verses.translation_literal: A psalm, of David, to bring to remembrance.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David, a song made for remembering.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the superscription, and in the Hebrew text it counts as verse 1; the KJV prints it unnumbered, so its verse 1 is our verse 2 and the whole psalm is shifted by one. Treat it as a stage direction for how the piece is to be used, not as part of the speech. 'Lehazkir' is a puzzle ancient readers already argued over: Rashi takes it as a prayer to be said in a time of distress, to put Israel's trouble in front of God; Radak and Meiri hear 'to give thanks' or 'to proclaim', as in Isaiah 12:4; Malbim hears the sinner calling his own sins to mind. The word may also be a musical or liturgical label, as in the heading of Psalm 70. The KJV's 'to bring to remembrance' is faithful to the form but, like the Hebrew, tells the reader nothing about who is to remember what. Play it open: the audience should not yet know whether the one remembered is the sufferer, his sin or God.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil infinitive of zakhar, 'to cause to remember'. The sense is disputed: a liturgical or musical term, 'to confess/proclaim', or a memorial of sin. Psalm 70 carries the same label.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, not in your anger may you rebuke me, and in your wrath [not] may you chasten me.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, do not correct me while you burn with anger; do not discipline me in the heat of your fury.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a plea, and the plea is a legal one. Two verbs of correction, rebuke and chasten, name what a father or a judge does to a son or a subject. The speaker does not deny that he may be corrected. He asks that it not be done in anger. The sufferer knows he is under judgment, and he is asking for its tone and its measure.

The Hebrew gives the negative once. אַל, 'not', stands at the head of the verse and has to be carried across to the second half, so that the line reads 'not in your anger rebuke me, and [not] in your wrath chasten me'. Radak and Metzudat David say so, and Meiri compares the same economy elsewhere in Scripture. The KJV smooths this by writing 'neither' in the second half, which is fair English but hides how compressed the Hebrew is: a man in pain does not spend words. The KJV also gives 'in thy wrath' and 'in thy hot displeasure' as two different pictures. The Hebrew words are קֶצֶף and חֵמָה, and both are heat words, with חֵמָה from the root for 'to be hot'. The pair says the same thing twice, with the second line raising the first. Play it as repetition from someone who cannot stop pleading.

The verse is also nearly the same as the opening of Psalm 6. A listener who knew that psalm would hear the echo at once: here is a prayer that has been prayed before, and it is the speaker's second chance to say it. The spelling בְּקֶצְפְּךָ with a segol under the ק has a segol where a hiriq would be expected, and Radak and Meiri note it, comparing Ps 128:3.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of יכח: to reprove, to decide a case, to set right. It is the verb of the courtroom and of the father's correction. Here the sufferer asks not to be corrected in anger.
Piel of יסר: to chasten, to discipline by pain, as a father with a child. It is a harder word than the first and lands on the body.

verses.translation_literal: For your arrows have come down in me, and your hand has come down on me.
verses.translation_dramatic: For your arrows have sunk deep into me, and your hand has come down upon me like a weight.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason for the plea is a double image of a divine archer and a divine hand. The root nachat ('to descend') is used twice, once for the arrows and once for the hand, so the verse literally says that arrows came down and a hand came down. The KJV's 'stick fast' and 'presseth me sore' are two different English phrases for one Hebrew verb, and they hide the echo. In the ancient Near East, arrows were a standard picture for the gods' sickness-sending: plague as divine archery is familiar from Mesopotamian and Greek sources, and the speaker is also using it in Job 6:4 and Deuteronomy 32:23. The 'hand' of God is the language of the blow and of the plague alike. Rashi's grammar note matters for the performer: the first verb looks Niphal, but the nun is not part of the root; the sense is the same, 'they came down'. Radak and Ibn Ezra read the arrows as sicknesses, Malbim as the inward arrows of despair against the outward hand of bodily blow. Let the actor hear the first line as a stab, the second as a press.

philological_notes.note: 'They came down, they sank in'. The same root begins the second line (vatinchat), so the repetition is deliberate. Rashi explains the form as having an assimilated nun; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as Niphal.
Your arrows. Radak and Meiri take them as the illnesses and troubles; Malbim as the inward arrows of despair.

verses.translation_literal: There is no soundness in my flesh from the face of your indignation; there is no peace in my bones from the face of my sin.
verses.translation_dramatic: There is nothing whole left in my flesh, because of your indignation; there is no rest in my very bones, because of my sin.
verses.directors_commentary: Two lines, built the same, name two causes: his flesh suffers 'from the face of your indignation', his bones 'from the face of my sin'. Hebrew 'mipnei' is literally 'from the face of', the language of a person standing before an angry superior, and the KJV's 'because of' flattens that. The first line is God's side, the second the speaker's: he does not say 'I am innocent' but names his own sin plainly, as Radak says, 'it is not for nothing'. 'Metom' means wholeness or soundness, the condition of an animal fit for the altar; 'shalom' is not just 'rest' (KJV) but completeness, the opposite of broken. Radak notes that bones are stronger than flesh and so, when even they lack peace, the pain is at its deepest; Malbim hears flesh as the outer body, bones as the inner self. The KJV uses 'anger' where the Hebrew has the rarer 'za'am', a word for indignation, a bit like a judge's, and then 'sin' for chatta't, which can also mean a failing. Say the two halves in the same voice, so that the sin is not cheaper than the blow.

philological_notes.note: Wholeness, soundness, an unblemished body. Radak records a second derivation from the root of 'metim' (few), with the sense that nothing of the human form was left.
Not only 'rest' but completeness, wellbeing: the opposite of broken. It echoes the 'soundness' of the first line.
Literally 'from the face of', as a subject stands before an angry master; ordinary usage reduces it to 'because of'.

verses.translation_literal: For my iniquities have passed over my head; like a heavy burden they are too heavy from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My guilt has risen over my head like floodwater, and like a crushing load it is heavier than I can bear.
verses.directors_commentary: Two pictures of guilt follow each other: water that has risen over the head, and a load too great for the carrier. The verb 'avar' is 'to pass over', the word for a flood sweeping over, as in Psalm 69:3 and 124:4; Radak and Metzudat David both read the first picture as drowning. The second picture uses one root twice, 'heavy burden... they are heavy' (masa kaved / yikhbedu), a repetition the KJV softens a little with 'too heavy for me'. The final word, 'mimmeni', is literally 'from me': too heavy, away from my strength. Meiri and Radak read that as 'I have too few good deeds to lighten the load'. The word 'avon' (iniquity) means both the crooked act and its penalty, so the burden is the guilt and its consequence in one. An actor can use the double sense: the sin is both what he did and what is now being done to him. The KJV's 'gone over mine head' is accurate; the old 'as an heavy burden' is archaic only in grammar.

philological_notes.note: 'Iniquities' in the plural. The noun carries both the crooked act and its consequence: guilt and punishment in one word.
A repeated root: 'like a heavy burden they are heavy'. Radak reads it as a load he has no strength to carry.

token_glosses.gloss: from me, too much for me

verses.translation_literal: They stink, they fester, my wounds, from the face of my folly.
verses.translation_dramatic: My wounds reek; they rot and run, and the cause is my own folly.
verses.directors_commentary: The images turn from drowning to the body, and the Hebrew is rawer than the KJV's 'stink and are corrupt'. The verbs come first, and bare: 'they stink, they fester'. 'Hiv'ishu' is the verb for a smell gone bad, used of the manna left overnight (Exodus 16:24) and of the dead fish of the Nile (Exodus 7:18). 'Namaqu' means to rot away, to melt; Radak describes the skin dissolving over a fluid-filled swelling until the liquid runs out and the smell spreads. 'Chaburah' is a bruise or weal, not a modern 'wound' in the sense of a clean cut. The KJV's 'corrupt' is an old word for decay and has been softened by time into a moral word; modern ears hear 'corrupt politician', not 'pus'. The cause is 'ivvalti', 'my folly': the word of the fool (evil), not the one who makes a mistake. Radak: folly as not guarding the way of the LORD. The speaker owns the shame; the audience should smell it.

philological_notes.note: Stinks, turns foul. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as an intransitive Hiphil, as in Exodus 16:24.
To rot away, to melt: the flesh breaks down under the skin. Metzudat Zion glosses it as melting.
Weals, bruises, blisters: a wound where blood or fluid gathers beneath the skin (Metzudat Zion). Isaiah 1:6 uses the same word of a body struck from head to foot.

verses.translation_literal: I am bent, I am bowed down, up to much; all the day mourning I go about.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am twisted and bowed to the ground; all day long I drag myself about in black.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the posture. The speaker walks bent over, and the Hebrew uses two near-synonyms for 'bent' back to back: 'na'aveiti' (twisted, crooked, from the root of 'avon', iniquity) and 'shachoti' (bowed down). The KJV's 'I am troubled' for the first misses the physical sense altogether: Rashi relates it to a cramp or spasm, Metzudat Zion to 'crooked', and the bend in the body is a bend in the soul, since the root is the same as 'iniquity'. 'Ad me'od', literally 'up to muchness', is the Hebrew idiom of extremity, and the KJV's 'greatly' is a fair rendering. 'Qoder' is dark, as in a sky gone black or a face covered in soot: mourners dress and darken themselves. 'Hilakhti', 'I have gone about', is a Piel form, an intensive: not a walk but a constant going back and forth. An actor can walk the verse bent double, since the Hebrew pictures a person who cannot straighten his back.

philological_notes.note: Bent, twisted, crooked; the same root gives 'avon' (iniquity, the crooked). Rashi connects it to a cramp.
Dark, blackened; the word for a mourner's dress and look. Radak says the face grew dark.

verses.translation_literal: For my loins are full of burning, and there is no soundness in my flesh.
verses.translation_dramatic: For my loins are full of fire, and nothing in my flesh is whole.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV gives 'loathsome disease', which is a guess dressed as a diagnosis. The form 'niqleh' can come from a root meaning 'to roast, scorch' (as in the 'roasted grain' of Leviticus 2:14), which Radak attributes to his father and Metzudat Zion and the Targum support, or from a root meaning 'to be despised', hence 'a despicable plague', Radak's own first choice and Meiri's. The KJV is following the second, though the first fits the context of fever better: it is the old translation's way of saying 'something shameful' without naming it. 'Kesalim' are the loins or flanks, the muscles of the lower back beside the kidneys, the seat of strength and, in Hebrew idiom, of the vital organs. 'Burning' therefore means a fevered lower body, and the repetition of 'there is no soundness in my flesh' from verse 4 is deliberate: Radak says it is the way of someone weeping and groaning to repeat himself. Do not let the actor lighten it; the second line is a refrain, said again because there is nothing else to say.

philological_notes.note: Disputed: either 'burning, scorching' (from the root of 'roasted grain', Lev 2:14) or 'despised, shameful' (an adjective with its noun left out). The first fits a fever; the second is the KJV's 'loathsome'.
The loins or flanks, the lower back next to the kidneys.

verses.translation_literal: I am faint and I am crushed up to much; I roar from the groaning of my heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am drained, I am crushed to powder, and from the groaning of my heart I roar.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the lowest point of the list of symptoms. The body is spent (נפוגותי), then broken (נדכיתי), and the verse ends with a sound. The sound is a roar: שאגתי is the word for a lion, and the Hebrew uses it for a sick man. The KJV's 'I have roared' keeps it. The ASV's 'groaned' softens it and loses the animal; the BBE's 'I gave a cry like a lion' adds a 'like' that the Hebrew does not have. The text says 'I roar', flat, with no comparison.

The roar comes 'from the groaning of my heart'. The noun נַהֲמָה is a growl or a murmur that rises from within, and the heart is the seat of mind as well as feeling. So the cry that others hear is the outward end of a sound the heart has been making in private. Radak reads it just so: the heart groans over the illness and the troubles, and the voice breaks out of it.

Ibn Ezra ties the lion to another sick man's prayer, in Isaiah 38:13: Hezekiah says, in his own illness, 'shiwwiti ad-boqer ka'ari', 'I composed myself until morning; like a lion...' (the verb is disputed, and the lines that follow are about bones being broken). Ibn Ezra's point is not that the two verses say the same thing, only that a sufferer in the Bible may be compared to a lion, and that here the roaring comes from the abundance of pains. Do not play it as a display. Play it as the sound that escapes a man too weak to hold it in.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of פוג: to grow numb, slack, faint. The same root is used of Jacob's heart in Gen 45:26 (ויפג לבו), when he hears that Joseph is alive and cannot take it in. Here the body goes slack. STEPBible's 'numb' is possible; 'faint' keeps the sense of weakness Rashi and Radak give it.
To roar, as a lion roars. The word is for the animal's cry; it is used of a man who cannot be silent. The Hebrew says 'I roar' without 'like'.

verses.translation_literal: My Lord, before you is all my desire, and my sighing from you is not hidden.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now, Lord, I turn back to you, after all I have told: everything I long for lies in front of you, and not one sigh of mine is hidden from you.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long description of the body in verses 5 to 9, the speaker turns his face back to God. He has been speaking to God since verse 2, but the 'your arrows' and 'your indignation' of verses 3 and 4 were spoken at God's hand rather than to God's face. Here he says the name again, and the voice softens. The divine name is different from verse 2: not YHWH but אֲדֹנָי, 'my Lord', a word of the servant for the master. The KJV writes 'Lord' for both, which blurs the shift.

The verse rests on two nouns, תַּאֲוָה (desire) and אֲנָחָה (sighing), and a verb that says what the sufferer fears most: that he is not seen. 'Is not hidden' answers it. Whatever has been unsaid or inaudible is there before God. Radak links this to the roar of verse 9: whether I roar or do not roar, you know the desire of my heart. What the desire is, the commentators do not agree. Ibn Ezra, followed by Radak, takes it as the wish to live, and adds 'to you alone, perhaps I shall live, not before the physicians'. Meiri takes it as the wish to serve God. Metzudat David takes it as the cure that is God's to give. The translation keeps the word wide, 'all my desire', so that any of these readings stays open for the actor.

The KJV 'is before thee' is accurate. The word נֶגֶד is 'in front of', 'in view of', and it puts the longing in God's sight and not only in his hearing. 'Groaning' for אֲנָחָה is a little strong in the KJV; 'sighing' (YLT) is closer, a breath let out rather than a cry.

philological_notes.note: 'In front of you', in your sight. The preposition puts the speaker's longing in the field of God's view.
Desire, longing. The commentators split on what it is: the wish to live (Ibn Ezra, Radak), the wish to serve God (Meiri), or the cure (Metzudat David). The Hebrew does not say.
A sigh, a breath let out in grief. It is quieter than the roar of verse 9.

verses.translation_literal: My heart goes round and round, my strength has left me, and the light of my eyes, even they are not with me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart spins and reels; my strength has left me, and even the light of my eyes is gone from me.
verses.directors_commentary: A body failing on three fronts: heart, strength, sight. 'Secharchar' is a reduplicated verb from 'sachar', 'to go around': Rashi compares it to doubled words like 'yeraqraq' (yellowish-green) and Radak glosses it as 'round and round', as in the Aramaic 'sachor sachor'. The KJV's 'panteth' and ASV's 'throbbeth' guess at a heartbeat; the Hebrew has the heart circling like a man who cannot find his way, or, in Radak's terms, a mind that goes round and round without rest. Next 'azavani kochi', 'my strength has abandoned me', where 'azav' is the verb of forsaking, the same word used of a friend or a god who leaves. The last line has a twist the KJV paraphrases away: 'gam hem', 'even they', plural, referring to the light of the eyes, as if the eyes' light were many things that have departed. Radak and Meiri note the same plural in 1 Samuel 2:4 and Job 29:10. Say 'even they' with a drop: of everything that left him, this is the one he did not expect.

philological_notes.note: A reduplicated form from 'to go around': the heart circles, spins. Rashi compares doubled forms such as yeraqraq.
'Even they': a plural pronoun after the singular 'light of my eyes'. Radak compares 1 Samuel 2:4 and Job 29:10 for the same construction.

verses.translation_literal: Those who love me and my companions stand away from before my plague, and my near ones have stood from a distance.
verses.translation_dramatic: Those who loved me, my friends, keep their distance from my affliction, and my own kin stand far off.
verses.directors_commentary: The last pain is social. The KJV's 'my lovers' is correct, but modern English hears it as erotic, so the dramatic text says 'those who loved me'. 'Ohavai' (those who love me) and 're'ai' (my companions) are two circles of intimacy, and 'qrovai' (my near ones, kin or neighbours) the third. They stand 'minneged', 'from in front of' (a stance of watching from across the way), and the verb is 'ya'amodu', 'they stand', then 'amadu', 'they have stood', so the standing is both present and a long habit. The key word is 'nega'', 'plague', which is the term of Leviticus 13 for a skin affliction that a priest examines and that sends a person outside the camp; the KJV's 'sore' removes that legal echo. The reader of the time would hear that the friends keep the distance a clean person keeps from a diseased one. Radak adds the human reason: the sight of a sick person is hard to bear, and a visit would have strengthened him; Rashi, that these were friends in good times only. The final word, 'amadu', ends the stanza on a stillness: they do nothing.

philological_notes.note: 'My plague, my stroke'. The same noun is used in Leviticus 13 for a skin affliction examined by a priest; the word brings isolation with it. Used here of the sufferer's wounds in general.
'From opposite, from before': the friends stand across from the sufferer, watching but not approaching. Rashi reads it as 'they do not help me'.

verses.translation_literal: And they lay snares, those seeking my life, and those seeking my harm have spoken ruinous things, and deceits all the day they murmur.
verses.translation_dramatic: They are setting their traps now, the ones who hunt my life. They who look for my hurt speak of my ruin in low voices, and all day long, all day, they mutter their lies to one another.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker is a sick man surrounded by watchers, and the verbs have to carry that. 'Seek my life' is the language of a manhunt (compare 1 Sam 22:23, which Radak cites), and the 'snare' is a bird-catcher's trap, set quietly and baited with words. The KJV's 'speak mischievous things' is far too mild: havvot means calamity, ruin, the kind of thing you say of a man you expect to fall. 'Imagine deceits' is also archaic; yehgu is the verb for murmuring or muttering, used elsewhere for low moaning and for meditating on the Torah, so the enemies are rehearsing their lies under their breath, all day. Rashi simply takes the snare as the plain sense, 'they set traps for me', while Metzudat David has the enemies speaking words that break the spirit. Play it as whisper, not shout.

philological_notes.note: A denominative verb from the noun for a snare or bait (moqesh): 'they lay snares'. Rashi paraphrases it as 'they set snares for me', and Metzudat David as 'they hid a trap for me'.
Plural of a noun meaning ruin or calamity. Radak glosses it as a language of breaking and of evil matters; the KJV 'mischievous things' loses the sense of disaster wished on the speaker.
To murmur, mutter or ponder. Rashi glosses it 'they think', but the verb is a vocal one. 'Imagine' in the KJV is a good word for the inner rehearsal and a poor one for the sound.

verses.translation_literal: And I, like a deaf man, I do not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I? I am as one who cannot hear. Their words go past me. I am as one who has no voice, whose mouth stays shut.
verses.directors_commentary: After the noise of the whisperers, silence. The speaker's answer to the plots is to hear nothing and say nothing, and the Hebrew gives us two clauses that are almost mirror images: deaf, not hearing; mute, not opening the mouth. The KJV's past tenses ('heard not', 'was') turn a present stance into a story; the Hebrew has imperfects, 'I do not hear', 'he does not open', which describe a habit of restraint, not a single moment. Whether this is real helplessness or chosen silence is the question the tradition splits on. Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri all say the man hears perfectly and makes himself deaf; Malbim adds that the enemies spoke in front of him because they thought he could not hear. Rashi hears Israel speaking: they take the insults and do not answer, because they wait on God. The actor should decide which, and let the audience see it in the body.

philological_notes.note: 'Like a deaf man.' The comparison is with deafness, not with sleep or ignorance, and the commentators say it is a pretence: Metzudat David has him 'making himself deaf, as if I did not hear'.
Mute, unable or unwilling to speak. Radak explains that he holds his tongue and does not answer the insults he hears.

verses.translation_literal: And I have become like a man who is not hearing, and there is not in his mouth arguments.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I became that man: a man who does not hear, and in whose mouth there is no answer, no argument, nothing to say back.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse repeats the thought of the one before and tightens it: the deaf man now has no 'reproofs' either. The KJV 'reproofs' is correct but sounds like a scolding; tokhachot is the language of the lawcourt and of debate, arguments a man would bring to prove his case (compare Isa 1:18, 'let us reason together', which Meiri cites for the root). So the silence is a refusal to go to law with his accusers. In a world without a neutral court for the sick and the shamed, you answered insults or you were taken to have conceded them; he chooses the risk. The 'I have become' (va'ehi) marks a settled change, not a pose for an afternoon. Malbim says plainly that he was not truly deaf: he made himself so, and did not fear the traps. Play the stillness as strength.

philological_notes.note: Arguments, rebuttals, the points a man would bring in a dispute. Meiri glosses it as 'pleas to answer them', tying it to 'let us reason together' in Isa 1:18; Metzudat David glosses it as arguments to contend with them.

verses.translation_literal: For for you, YHWH, I have waited; you, you will answer, O Lord my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Because it is for you, O LORD, that I have waited. You, and only you, will answer, my Lord, my God.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm, and it explains the silence: he does not answer them because he is waiting for someone else to. The Hebrew places 'for you' first and then says 'you' again before the verb, 'you, you will answer', so the pronoun is doubled for emphasis; no English translation carries that except by stress. The KJV renders ta'aneh as 'thou wilt hear', softening a word that means 'answer', often in the sense of a legal reply, and Metzudat David takes it as God answering the enemies on his behalf, with a sign for good that is a winning rebuttal. Radak has the speaker say, 'Why should I argue with them? I have no hope in them, only in you alone.' The verb hochalti is waiting with expectation, not idle delay. And then three names pile up: YHWH, Adonai, my God. A man who has said nothing to anyone all day now lets the names pour out.

philological_notes.note: To wait, to hope, with the expectation that the waiting will be met. Metzudat Zion links it to 'and I waited for your words' in Job 32.
'You will answer', and not merely 'hear'. Metzudat David reads the answer as God's reply to the enemies for him: 'you will do a sign for good and it will count as a winning answer'.

verses.translation_literal: For I said, Lest they rejoice over me; when my foot slips, over me they have made themselves great.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I told myself: let them not rejoice over me. Because the moment my foot slipped, they swelled up against me, so proud.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV puts 'Hear me' into the speaker's mouth ('For I said, Hear me, lest...'); there is nothing like it in the Hebrew, which has simply 'I said, lest they rejoice'. What he said, in his heart, is a fear: that his enemies will gloat. 'Rejoice over me' is not neutral happiness; it is the triumphant joy of the man who sees a rival fall. The foot that 'slips' is the stumble of a man on a rocky path or a wet step, and it stands for any failure; the verb higdilu, 'they made themselves great', is from the root 'big', so the enemies puff up the instant he wobbles. Radak and Metzudat David both read the logic as: if even a slight stumble made them boast, what would they do if I fell altogether? Rashi has the people say the same of themselves: we keep silent, lest they see us fall and exult. The verse is the reason for the earlier silence.

philological_notes.note: 'When my foot slips', and the noun is the infinitive of a verb for tottering or swaying. Metzudat Zion ties it to Deut 32:35, 'at the time their foot slips'.
Causative of 'to be great': 'they magnified themselves', that is, they boasted. Metzudat David reads it as 'they made themselves proud against me'; Ibn Ezra notes the verb may also be about speech.

verses.translation_literal: For I, for limping I am set, and my pain is before me continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I am ready to fall, ready for the limp, and my pain stands in front of me every moment, and never leaves.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Ready to halt' is the KJV's word, and 'halt' here is old English for 'limp', so the English reader today hears 'stop' and misses the point. Tsela' is the lame gait of a man whose leg or hip has been struck, and nakhon is 'set, established, prepared': he is not about to limp, he is fixed in it, as a man is fixed in a stance. Ibn Ezra says it plainly: he is so prepared for lameness that he cannot rise for many days. Rashi reads it as a people trained by blows and always ready for the next. 'My pain is before me' (negdi) is spatial, a thing in the line of sight, the way a debt or a witness stands before you. 'Continually' (tamid) is the word of the daily offering, the one that never lapses. Stage him at the edge of a fall that never ends.

philological_notes.note: A limp. Metzudat Zion glosses the verb as the lame man leaning on his thigh; Metzudat David reads it as his body weak and used to limping.
Continually, without break; the same word names the daily burnt offering. The pain, like that offering, never lapses.

verses.translation_literal: For my iniquity I declare; I am anxious from my sin.
verses.translation_dramatic: For my guilt I will not hide. I say it aloud. And I am sick with worry over my sin.
verses.directors_commentary: In the middle of a psalm of enemies, the speaker turns and says: I am not innocent. The verb is aggid, 'I declare, I tell', the verb of open confession, and it follows the silence of the earlier verses, so what he refuses to say to his accusers he says here to God. The KJV 'I will be sorry' is a thin rendering of de'ag, which is anxiety, a gnawing dread; the same root names the worry of Saul's father in 1 Sam 9:5. Notice the preposition: he is anxious 'from' his sin, afraid of what it will bring. Radak says he fears that it may become a trap for him; Rashi that it may cause his limp and pain. Metzudat David reads it as fear that the punishment will come and his enemies will rejoice. This verse should be the quietest and most personal in the window.

philological_notes.note: Causative: 'I make known, I declare.' It is the verb of telling, here of confession to God, and Metzudat David reads it as 'I myself tell my iniquity, for I know that I have sinned'.
To be anxious or afraid. 'Sorry' in the KJV does not carry the fear that the verb has.

verses.translation_literal: And my enemies, alive, are mighty, and many are those who hate me falsely.
verses.translation_dramatic: But my enemies are alive, vigorous, strong, and they grow in number, those who hate me for a lie.
verses.directors_commentary: The contrast is the point: he limps, and they thrive. The first clause is hard. 'Alive, they are mighty' (chayyim atsemu) can mean 'in full life they are strong'; the KJV's 'lively' is archaic and now sounds merry, when the sense is robust health and prosperity. Rashi reads it as 'they grow strong in life, in peace and in good'; Meiri says they are healthy and at ease; Radak adds that they have children and wealth while he is poor and crushed. Some readers take the wording as a textual puzzle, and Ibn Ezra records that some link it to the fear of dying while the enemies live on. 'Falsely' (sheqer) is a lie: Radak glosses it 'for nothing, without cause', citing 1 Sam 25:21, so they hate him for no reason. The KJV 'wrongfully' captures that. Note the line of the man's reasoning: I am guilty before God, yet their hatred is groundless.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'alive, they are mighty'. A known difficulty; the commentators read it as vigorous life and ease (Rashi, Radak, Meiri). Metzudat Zion cites the root's sense of multiplying, as in Jer 15:8.
A lie, falsehood; here the hatred is groundless. Radak glosses it 'for nothing' and cites 1 Sam 25:21.

verses.translation_literal: And [those] repaying evil in place of good, they accuse me, in place of my pursuing good.
verses.translation_dramatic: They pay me back in evil for the good I gave. They set themselves against me, they stand as my accusers, and the only charge is this: that I went after what is good.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a man pointing out the plain injustice of his case, not as self-praise. The ledger language is commercial: shillem is to pay back or settle an account, and tachat, 'in place of', sets the two sides of the exchange against each other, evil for good, as if a debt were being settled in the wrong coin. In the ancient Near East a benefit given was expected to be answered with loyalty, so returning harm for kindness is a breach of the most basic reciprocity. Tachat then appears a second time, and the speaker turns it on the enemies' motive: they accuse him in place of, that is, because of, his pursuing good.

The verb yistenuni is the quiet sting. It comes from the root of satan, 'adversary' or 'accuser', so the enemies take up the role of a hostile prosecutor against him. The KJV says 'are mine adversaries', which turns the action into a state, and its 'because I follow the thing that good is' is clumsy English for a plain Hebrew phrase, 'pursuing good'. YLT's 'accuse' is nearer the verb. The speaker's verb, radaf, 'pursue', is the same word used for chasing an enemy, so his chosen target is good where his enemies' target is him: in v.13 they 'seek' his life and speak of his harm, and in v.20 the haters multiply. Notice too that the text reads radefi but is written radofi; the reading is an infinitive, 'my pursuing', and Radak and Meiri explain the lengthened vowel by comparison with yorde bor, 'those going down to the pit' (Ps 30:4).

philological_notes.note: A verb built on the root of satan, 'adversary': they act as accusers or opponents against me. Metzudat Zion links it to sitnah, enmity and the nursing of hatred, as in vayistom Esau, 'and Esau bore a grudge', which he cites.

The Qere reads an infinitive with my-suffix, 'my pursuing'; the Ketiv radofi is written with a vav. Radak and Meiri compare the lengthened resh in yorde bor (Ps 30:4). The verb 'pursue' is the same one used of chasing enemies, here applied to good.

token_glosses.gloss: they accuse me, they play the adversary against me

verses.translation_literal: Do not forsake me, YHWH; my God, do not be far from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not leave me, O LORD. My God, do not stand far off from me.
verses.directors_commentary: The long account of enemies and guilt ends in a plain double plea, built as two prohibitions: al ta'azveni, 'do not forsake me', and al tirchak, 'do not be far'. The first is abandonment; the second is distance. The two negatives are the same particle (al) that begins a prayer and not a statement, so this is a request, not a report. The KJV renders 'be not far from me' rightly; the BBE 'be near' turns a negative into a positive. In the ancient world a god who was far was a god who had withdrawn his protection, and the Hebrew verb 'forsake' is what the enemies expect to happen. Radak says it means 'as they think I have no helper', and Metzudat David that, since he cannot answer them, God should be his answer to their mockery. Ibn Ezra notes it answers the earlier line that his friends stood at a distance. The names again pile up: YHWH, my God.

philological_notes.note: 'Do not be far.' It answers the complaint of distance in the earlier verses and Ibn Ezra reads it against 'they stood afar off'.

verses.translation_literal: Hurry to my help, O Lord, my salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hurry. Come quickly to help me, O Lord, my rescue, my only salvation.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends not with a resolution but a command in the imperative: chushah, 'hurry'. It is a short, breathless word, one of the few verbs of haste in the Psalms, and the Hebrew's rhythm gives it no room to breathe. The KJV 'make haste' is correct but long. The last word is a title as much as a name: 'Lord, my salvation', and Ibn Ezra and Radak both take it as 'you who are my salvation', with Meiri allowing that it might be either 'the God of my salvation' or 'my salvation itself'. For the singer, rescue is not something God gives; it is who God is. Note the arc of the whole section: whisper, silence, waiting, confession, a plea not to be left, and then this one word of haste. The scene ends with him still limping, still surrounded, still waiting.

philological_notes.note: 'Hurry!' An imperative with the ending -ah, a verb of urgent haste. Radak glosses it simply as 'hurry'.
'My salvation', as a title for God. Ibn Ezra and Meiri allow 'you are my salvation' or 'the God of my salvation'.
